article.overview: An infrared telescope is an astronomical instrument that collects infrared radiation, light with wavelengths longer than visible red light, and focuses it onto a detector. Infrared observations reveal cool dust, young stars forming inside gas clouds and the redshifted light of very distant galaxies, much of which is hard or impossible to observe from the ground. On the Moon, interest in infrared telescopes rests on two features: the Moon has no atmosphere to absorb and emit infrared radiation, and its permanently shadowed craters near the poles are naturally very cold, which could allow passive cooling [1][2]. As far as the sources reviewed for this article show, no infrared telescope has yet operated from the Moon. The closest flown precedent is the Apollo 16 Far Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph, an ultraviolet instrument [3][4]. The nearest near-term infrared hardware, L-CIRiS, is a planned infrared camera for surface mapping rather than an astronomical telescope [5].
article.description: An infrared telescope has the same basic parts as an optical telescope: a collector (a mirror or lens) that gathers light, optics that focus it, and a detector that converts it into an electrical signal. Infrared work differs in two practical ways. First, detectors and the telescope's own structure emit heat, which can swamp faint infrared signals, so far-infrared telescopes are normally cooled to very low temperatures. Second, Earth's atmosphere blocks much of the infrared spectrum, which is why infrared astronomy is usually carried out from space or from very high, dry sites. Proposed lunar infrared telescopes would use the lack of atmosphere and, in permanently shadowed craters, the cold surroundings to reduce the active cooling required. A Space.com report of one proposal quotes its proposer saying that the maximum infrared limit comes from the temperature to which the telescope can be cooled [6]. No flown lunar infrared telescope is described in the sources reviewed.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main scientific case for a lunar infrared telescope is access to wavelengths that are difficult to observe well from Earth or from existing space telescopes. One proposal, described in conference abstracts, is a general-purpose collector covering roughly 1 to 200 µm, with a far-infrared instrument aimed at cosmic microwave background spectral distortions [2]. The far-infrared band is where astronomers hope to study the earliest stages of galaxy formation, and the proposers say that no existing telescope can observe up to about 200 µm [2][6]. A second application is interferometry. The Silk et al. review notes that a lunar platform's stability could allow integration times of hours, compared with milliseconds for terrestrial beam-combining interferometers, but it gives no infrared interferometer design figures [1].
article.operating_principle: A lunar infrared telescope would collect incoming infrared radiation, focus it, pass it through filters or a spectrometer, and record it with a detector. For far-infrared work the detector and optics must be cold enough that their own thermal emission does not drown out the faint astronomical signal. Passive cooling uses a shadowed, cold surface to reject heat without power-consuming refrigeration. The Silk et al. review describes polar craters as naturally very cold and cites temperatures down to about 30 K there, but in the context of seismometers, not telescopes [1]. Whether a telescope inside such a crater could reach the temperatures needed for far-infrared work is a design question the sources reviewed do not settle. The sources also do not describe the optical configuration of the proposed far-infrared telescope. The L-CIRiS camera works on a different principle: it measures infrared emission from the surface to estimate temperature and composition, and its detector type is not stated in the LASP description [5].
article.scientific_importance: Infrared astronomy has been developed largely from space and high-altitude facilities, and the far-infrared window remains one of the least explored parts of the spectrum. The Silk et al. review records no flown infrared instrument among lunar payloads; the flown or scheduled payloads it mentions are radio instruments [1]. A lunar infrared telescope would therefore be a new capability rather than a continuation of an established lunar observatory. Its value depends on verified cooling performance, stable pointing and dust-free optics, none of which is demonstrated on the Moon in the sources reviewed.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for an infrared telescope or infrared camera. The three examples below belong to different categories: a flown ultraviolet telescope, a planned infrared imaging camera and a proposed far-infrared telescope. Their numbers are not comparable, and none of them should be read as a specification for a generic infrared telescope.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: For the proposed far-infrared telescope, the reported upper bound is a 13 m diameter, cited in the Silk et al. review as allowing an installation of up to that size in a polar crater using ESA's ARGONAUT transporter concept. The Apollo 16 camera's optical aperture is 7.5 cm. No dimensions are verified for L-CIRiS. Dimensions for any new infrared telescope would depend on the wavelength range, collecting area and transport vehicle, none of which is fixed by these sources.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass is not stated in the sources reviewed for any of the three examples. The mass of the Apollo 16 camera is not given in the NASA or NTRS record read for this article.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power requirements are not stated for any example in the sources reviewed. The Apollo camera was operated by astronauts, and the L-CIRiS power budget is not published in the LASP description.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar infrared telescope would face the general lunar environment: no atmosphere, large temperature swings between day and night, radiation and micrometeoroid exposure. Permanently shadowed craters offer a very cold and stable thermal environment, but dark craters also raise concerns. The Silk et al. review flags lunar dust, which can be electrostatically levitated and deposited, as a concern for telescopes sited in dark craters, and notes that the meteoroid flux near the poles needs evaluation [1]. The L-CIRiS design target of -170 °C to +100 °C reflects the surface temperature range expected at the lunar poles [5]. Operational requirements such as pointing stability, cryogenic management and survival through the lunar night are not specified for any infrared telescope in the sources reviewed.
article.limitations: No infrared telescope has been flown or operated on the Moon according to the sources reviewed. The far-infrared design is a proposal, and no mass, cost, sensitivity or thermal budget is published in the sources read. Passive cooling in permanently shadowed craters is argued by proposers but not demonstrated. Dust, meteoroid exposure and pointing stability are open concerns [1]. Dark craters may also overlap with water-ice resource targets, which could create competition for the same sites [1]. The L-CIRiS description gives its temperature range and spatial resolution, but not its wavelength range or detector design [5].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A lunar infrared telescope would be delivered as a surface payload, either as a dedicated instrument or as part of a larger lander payload. The sources reviewed give a historical example of astronaut deployment and a planned robotic lander delivery for an infrared camera, but no verified interface data for any infrared telescope.
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument with the lander or transporter on Earth.
Launch it on a launch vehicle and transfer it towards the Moon.
Land it using a lunar lander, or install it with astronaut or robotic support.
Deploy and orient it, then establish thermal, mechanical, power and data interfaces.
For a far-infrared telescope in a polar crater, a large transporter concept would be needed; this is a proposed concept only.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The Apollo 16 camera was set up on the surface by the astronauts, placed in the shadow of the lunar module and re-oriented several times during the stay [4]. L-CIRiS is a planned ride-along on the CP-22 lander, with a mounting arrangement not described in the LASP page read [5]. The far-infrared proposal depends on the ESA ARGONAUT transporter concept cited in the Silk et al. review [1].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Apollo 16 Far Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph, flown in April 1972, is the historical precedent: an ultraviolet telescope set up and oriented by astronauts [3][4].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Compatibility with a named lander has not been verified. The LASP page for L-CIRiS names the CP-22 lander provider but does not give mass, mounting, power or data interface figures. No interface verification has been carried out for any infrared telescope in the sources reviewed.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo 16 Far Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph, built by George Carruthers and flown in April 1972, is described by NASA as the first telescope used for astronomical observations from the surface of another planetary body. Its crew returned 178 film frames of targets including star clusters, nebulae, the Large Magellanic Cloud and Earth's upper atmosphere [4]. The instrument was ultraviolet, not infrared, so it is not an infrared lunar telescope. It does, however, establish the practice of astronomy from the lunar surface, and NASA states that it remains on the Moon in the Descartes highlands [3][4].

article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The main uncertainty is that most of the infrared lunar telescope material is at concept level. The Maillard paper [2] could not be read in full because the publisher page returned HTTP 403 when accessed for this article. Its figures therefore come from conference-abstract summaries and press coverage [2][6]. The 18 K figure for some polar craters is reported in a press interview and was not verified in the primary paper [6]. Other lunar infrared concepts from earlier studies, including a liquid-mirror telescope proposal and a multi-element optical/infrared array, appear only in secondary search summaries. They are not described here as verified designs. The L-CIRiS schedule and design are based on LASP's current page and may change. Older coverage gives a different lander and launch date; those details are not used. The Apollo 16 focal ratio and mass are not in the NASA or NTRS sources read. The Smithsonian object page could not be accessed (HTTP 403), so no museum-held hardware details are used.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery.

data_quality_notes: No infrared telescope has been flown or operated from the Moon according to the sources reviewed. All infrared lunar telescope designs in this article are concepts.
The Maillard paper (Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 382, 20230070) could not be read in full: the publisher page returned HTTP 403. Its figures are taken from abstract-level summaries and press coverage.

The 18 K minimum crater temperature is reported in a press interview and was not verified in the primary paper. The Silk et al. review cites about 30 K for permanently shadowed craters in a seismometer context only.
Liquid-mirror and multi-element optical/infrared array concepts appear only in secondary search summaries and are not included as verified designs.

L-CIRiS is a planned infrared imaging camera rather than an astronomical telescope. Its detector type, wavelength range, mass, dimensions and power are not stated in the LASP page read. A search summary claim that it uses an uncooled microbolometer was not confirmed on the LASP page and is not used.
Older L-CIRiS coverage names a different lander and launch date; these outdated details are not used.
The Smithsonian object page for the Apollo 16 camera returned HTTP 403 and was not used as a source.
Apollo 16 camera focal ratio, focal length, field of view and mass are not stated in the NASA or NTRS sources read and are recorded as null.
Image URLs were checked to return HTTP 200 image/jpeg on the date of drafting; full-resolution downloads were not checked.
Lunar location recommendations are deferred by the user and are not included.
